title: Neurorobotics
summary:
Neurorobotics is the combined study of neuroscience, robotics, and artificial intelligence. It is the science and technology of embodied autonomous neural systems. Neural systems in neurorobotics include brain-inspired algorithms such as connectionist networks, computational models of biological neural networks such as artificial spiking neural networks and large-scale simulations of neural microcircuits, and actual biological systems including in vivo and in vitro neural nets. Such neural systems can be embodied in machines with mechanic or other forms of physical actuation, including robots, prosthetic or wearable systems, micro-machines, and even furniture and infrastructures.

Neurorobotics is based on the idea that the brain is embodied and the body is embedded in the environment. Therefore, most neurorobots are required to function in the real world, as opposed to a simulated environment.

Neurorobots can be divided into various major classes based on the robot's purpose. Each class is designed to implement a specific mechanism of interest for study. Common types include those used to study motor control, memory, action selection, and perception. Neurorobots used for motor control study motor feedback and control systems, and have proved their merit in developing controllers for robots. Locomotion is modeled by a number of neurologically inspired theories on the action of motor systems.

Neurorobots in memory studies are presented with simple mazes or patterns to learn. Some problems include recognition of symbols, colors, or other patterns and executing simple actions based on the pattern. Action selection studies deal with negative or positive weighting to an action and its outcome. Neurorobots can be used to study simple ethical interactions, though more commonly they contend with simpler tasks such as self-preservation or perpetuation of the population of robots.

The field of neurorobotics started in the late 1980s. Kawato and colleagues built a series of robotic devices to test how the cerebellum adapts movements. Gerald Edelman's group tested the Theory of Neuronal Group Selection by introducing the Darwin series of automata. Biological robots are not officially neurorobots in that they are not neurologically inspired AI systems, but actual neuron tissue wired to a robot, employing the use of cultured neural networks to study brain development or neural interactions.
